title: A Comparison of Choral and Individual Responding https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/epdf/10.1080/1045988X.2012.682184?needAccess=true
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 15, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This page summarizes Haydon, Marsicano, and Scott's literature review comparing choral and individual responding across six single-subject-design studies of students, mostly those with disabilities, on measures of engagement, on-task behavior, and academic performance. The authors conclude that choral responding, especially in whole-group settings, generally produces higher rates of active student responding, more correct responses, and better on-task behavior than individual responding. They also identify ways to strengthen choral responding further, including mixed responding, the model-lead-test procedure, appropriate scaffolding, and unison hand-raising. Barton's summary is careful to flag the review's limitations, only six studies and no quantitative effect-size analysis, so the conclusions are described as preliminary rather than definitive. The practical guidance is contingent on context: choral responding suits whole-group instruction on shared skills, while individual responding fits better when students are working at different levels on distinct skills.
points: Choral responding, especially during whole-group instruction, generally increases active student responding, correct responses, and on-task behavior compared with individual responding.

Mixed responding — interspersing individual checks within group choral responses — is recommended as a way to verify individual understanding without losing the engagement benefits of unison response.

Choose the strategy based on instructional context: group unison responding fits shared-skill whole-group teaching, while individual responding suits students working at different levels on distinct skills.
The evidence base is thin — six studies, no effect-size analysis — so Barton frames the findings as preliminary rather than a settled conclusion.
quotes: This research article reviews the literature comparing the effects of choral and individual responding on student engagement, on-task behavior, and academic performance.
The authors conclude that choral responding, especially in whole-group settings, generally leads to higher levels of active student responding and improved on-task behaviour.
Teachers can enhance and improve the effectiveness of group unison responding, particularly choral responding, by using mixed responding.
If all students in a large group need to learn the same skills, group unison responding may be appropriate.

On the basis of the results of this review, choral responding is seen to be a generally more effective instructional strategy than individual responding in terms of increasing active student responding.
